title: Sodom Falls and Lot Escapes
overview: Two messengers rescue Lot and his family from Sodom just before the LORD destroys it, and the chapter ends with Lot's daughters having children by their father.

parts.label: Lot takes in the strangers (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Lot is sitting in the city gate, where elders met and settled disputes, which may mean he had some standing in Sodom (v. 1). He insists that the two visitors, apparently two of the three who came to Abraham in chapter 18, stay with him rather than in the open square, and he feeds them as a good host was expected to do.

parts.label: The mob at the door (vv. 4-9)
parts.note: The men of Sodom, young and old, demand the guests in order to rape them. Older translations say 'know them', and v. 8 shows this means sex. Lot shields his guests but offers the mob his two daughters instead. This is a terrible betrayal of his own children, and the text does not approve it. The men mock him as a foreigner and rush the door (v. 9).

parts.label: Pulled to safety (vv. 10-16)
parts.note: The visitors pull Lot inside, blind the attackers, and say the LORD sent them to destroy the city because of the outcry against it (v. 13), probably the cries of the people it harmed. Lot's sons-in-law think he is joking (v. 14; translations differ on whether they were only engaged to his daughters), and when Lot hesitates, the visitors lead the family out by the hand, an act the text credits to the LORD's mercy (v. 16).

parts.label: Lot bargains for Zoar (vv. 17-22)
parts.note: Told to run for the mountains without looking back, Lot instead pleads to shelter in a nearby town, and the visitor agrees to spare it. The town's name, Zoar, sounds like the Hebrew word for 'small', which is why the narrator links it to Lot's plea that it is only a little place (vv. 20-22).

parts.label: Fire, salt and smoke (vv. 23-29)
parts.note: The LORD rains burning sulfur on Sodom, Gomorrah and the whole plain, killing everyone in the cities, and Lot's wife, for reasons the text does not give, looks back and becomes a pillar of salt (vv. 24-26). From where he had pleaded for the city in chapter 18, Abraham sees only smoke, and the narrator says Lot was saved because God 'remembered Abraham' (v. 29).

parts.label: Lot's daughters in the cave (vv. 30-38)
parts.note: Afraid to stay in Zoar, Lot lives in a mountain cave. His daughters believe no man is left to give them children, so on two nights they get him drunk and each sleeps with him without his awareness (vv. 31-36). Their sons become the ancestors of Moab and Ammon, Israel's neighbors, and since the text passes no verdict, scholars debate whether the story mocks those peoples' origins or simply explains them.

disagreement: Christians differ on what Sodom's sin was. Traditional teaching in Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant churches, often citing Jude 7, sees same-sex acts as central, usually alongside the violence. Others, including many modern scholars, point to the attempted gang rape here and to Ezekiel 16:49's charge of arrogance and neglect of the poor, and read the sin as violent cruelty to outsiders. Jewish tradition has stressed both. Rabbinic writings dwell on Sodom's cruelty to strangers and the poor, while some earlier Jewish writers also stressed sexual sin.
think: Have you ever struggled to leave a place or a part of your life even after you knew it was time to go, and what held you there?
